newsitem.title: USA: Anti-inflation drive seen test of independent Fed.
newsitem.headline: Anti-inflation drive seen test of independent Fed.

text.p: The Federal Reserve's independence may be put to the test amid criticism its drive against the roots of inflation could kill the American economic dream, analysts said on Friday.

"The Fed is in a very difficult environment because the Humphrey-Hawkins Act requires the Fed to seek full employment, maximum growth and price stability, and that's what we have," said Joe Carson, fixed-income chief economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, commenting on a March drop in the jobless rate to 5.2 percent.
"Without an anti-inflation mandate, the Fed is going to be seen as anti-jobs, anti-wages, anti-stocks. Greenspan is in a very difficult environment," Carson added.
The Fed last week took the "prudent step" to raise the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent.
Republican House Speaker Newt Gingrich said on Friday "it is unconscionable to have the Federal Reserve System close off economic growth because of some theoretical model."
Gingrich referred to the Phillips Curve theory that shows inflation as the outcome of an economy creating too many jobs and growing above its 2.0- to 2.5-percent trend rate.

Gingrich said the Congress will ask Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan, a Republican, to propose economic and fiscal changes that would allow the economy to expand by 4.0 or 5.0 percent without fueling inflation.

"There have been people in the Republican Party pushing that line for a long time. But the arguments are not very persuasive from an economic point of view," said former Fed vice chairman Alan Blinder.
Conservative Republicans last year blocked the nomination of investment banker Felix Rohatyn to the Fed Board because he supported the notion trend growth tops the 2.5-percent rate.

"You do get criticized when you raise interest rates. It's part of the territory. That's why we give the central bank independence," said Blinder, now who holds the chair of economics at Princeton University.
Blinder called the Fed's concern about the risks of two straight years of potentially above-trend growth "not an unwarranted fear, certainly not an unconscionable one."
"Nobody has any serious reason to temper with the independence of the Federal Reserve. It has been working extremely well to the benefit of everybody," added Blinder.
Fed officials shared the view of their former peer.
"The Chairman told Congress about policy objectives. We're not going to repeat we're not anti-growth every time someone accuses us of being anti-growth," a source at the Fed said.
Lou Crandall, chief economist at Wrightson and Associates, admitted that "no one wants to be associated with austerity."

"It's only the people who are down to the ultimate sound-bite level who criticize the rate hike. It's a great soap-box," Crandall noted. "Main street is telling us things are still great, consumer confidence remains high. It's those in the stock market who wish Greenspan would crawl back into his cave."
Crandall also said he believed criticism from Congress or Wall Street analysts will have little impact on the Fed.

"The reason why the Fed has remained independent all these years is because austerity is sometime necessary. Gingrich reflects the annoyance of people who lost money in the stock market last week," Crandall also said, adding that the preemptive, gradual nature of the rate hikes would lessen their psychological "shock" effect on the public.
But Nomura Securities International chief economist David Resler said the question of where the trend growth stands remains wide open.

"There still is a constituency for fighting inflation. But there is a legitimate disagreemnent about the speed at which the economy can grow," said Resler who points out the U.S. labor force has been recently growing at twice its expected pace, based on demographic expansion.
Such an increase could mean the non-inflationary growth trend may be clearly above 2.5 percent -- though for a limited period only.

"There are those who feel it's worth the gamble to see why we can't grow at 3.0 percent for a while longer," Resler pointed out. "There are those who feel the inflationary potential of the current growth is not that high, and that if inflation starts creeping into the economy, it still is time to act."
